title: Trial of the Knights Templar: Mass Diabolism by Torture
description: Between 1307 and 1314, Philip IV of France and Pope Clement V orchestrated the destruction of the Knights Templar, extracting confessions of idol worship, denial of Christ, sodomy, and obscene kisses through systematic torture. Over 600 Templars were arrested in France in October 1307, and hundreds confessed under torture to worshipping a demonic idol called Baphomet, urinating on the cross, and engaging in obscene initiation ceremonies. Jacques de Molay and other leaders were burned in 1314. The Templar trial demonstrated on a massive scale how torture could produce elaborate, consistent false confessions of diabolical practice, and established a precedent — familiar to all educated Europeans — that seemingly respectable Christians could secretly practice demonic worship. This precedent directly informed the credulity that enabled the witch trials.
historiographical_note: Norman Cohn in Europe's Inner Demons (1975) drew an explicit parallel between the Templar trial and the witch trials, arguing both demonstrated how judicial torture combined with elite belief in diabolical conspiracy could manufacture evidence of non-existent crimes. Malcolm Barber's The Trial of the Templars (1978) remains the standard modern study, documenting the political motivations and procedural irregularities.
source_method: Published trial records; parliamentary registers; secondary scholarship on the Templar trial
